newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bomb defendant wants death penalty dropped.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bomb defendant wants death penalty dropped.

text.p: Lawyers for Oklahoma City bombing defendant Terry Nichols filed court papers on Tuesday seeking to avoid the death penalty in the event he is found guilty.
Nichols argues that if convicted he should not be executed because he is accused only of being an accomplice and conspirator rather than the principal who committed the crime.
His lawyers argued in a court filing that a judge should declare the Federal Death Penalty Act of 1994 to be invalid in Nichols' case before jury selection begins on Sept. 29.

Nichols is accused of conspiring with and aiding former army buddy Timothy McVeigh to blow up the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City. The April 19, 1995, blast killed 168 people. McVeigh was convicted in June and sentenced to die.
A 1987 Supreme Court ruling forbids execution of an accomplice unless he was a major participant and showed a "reckless indifference to human life," Nichols' lawyers said.
They said evidence will show "that no rational juror could find beyond a reasonable doubt either that Mr. Nichols was recklessly indifferent to human life or that he was a major participant..."
Nichols is charged with helping McVeigh obtain bomb components, using proceeds from stolen guns to finance the bombing and helping build the truck bomb that McVeigh drove to Oklahoma City.

Nichols' lawyers said McVeigh was "proved to be the principal in the crime. But there is no dispute that Mr. Nichols was at home with his family, hundreds of miles away, when the explosion occurred..."
